b:
The Mother of the Sea - Sassuma Arnaa is a traditional Kalaallit tale. It goes something like this:
The People from Kalaallit Nunaat have always relied on animals from the sea for hunting.

Their ancestors were respecting the land and the balance with the sea, but according to the tale, this balance has been lost. Today, the people take too much from the sea without respecting it, polluting it, disregarding some parts of the animal without eating it completely.

The Mother of the Sea would get her hair messy with pollution, trapping the animals inside it. This would punish people for such disrespect by keeping the animals by her side, in the deep, not allowing them to go by the land. Thus hurting the hunting season for humans. One hunting season turned out to be so bad they wouldn’t even catch one animal, not even one seal.
One shaman, Angakkoq, would get ready to try and convince Sassuma Arnaa to release the animals.

He would sit with his hands tied behind his back and go into trance. While in a trance, his spirit would travel down to the deepness of the Sea, begging the Mother of the Sea for forgiveness, begging her to let him comb her hair, to clean the pollution and release the animals from it.
The shaman learns it was humans and their ways that prevented the animals from going to land all along, and promises to learn from this to avoid famine in the future.
It is this scene of the encounter of Angakkoq the shaman with Sassuma Arnaa which is depicted on this statue in the old Colonial harbor of Nuuk.

The statue was realized by Kalaalit artist Christian "Nuunu" Rosing in 2007, and the emplacement has been chosen perfectly for the tale, as the statue is standing in an intertidal zone, which means it lays below water levels half of the time, only fully visible at low tide.
